**Internal Memo — Engineering**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Buy more GPU hardware, or get more out of what we have?
**Date:** This week

We've reached the point in our capacity planning where the easy answer and the right answer have diverged. Our inference cluster is running hot during business hours, batch jobs are queuing into the evening, and the obvious instinct is to open a purchase order. Before we do that, I want to argue for a different sequence: spend the next quarter measurably improving utilisation of the hardware we already own, and treat new purchases as a follow-on decision made with better information.

The cost case for buying is straightforward on the surface. Our current fleet was acquired when prices and lead times were both worse than they are today, and the marginal cost of adding capacity has fallen. But the sticker price of a new node is only the beginning. There's power and cooling, rack space we'd need to negotiate for, the engineering time to integrate and monitor the new hardware, and — less visibly — the commitment we make to a particular accelerator family for the next three to four years. In a market where model architectures and serving stacks are shifting every few months, that commitment is a real liability. Buying hardware is one of the least reversible decisions we can make; the resale market for used accelerators is thin, and what we buy in March will be mid-generation by the time it's racked.

Utilisation, by contrast, is almost entirely reversible. Every scheduling improvement, every quantisation win, every batching refinement is a change we can undo, tune, or replace as our workload evolves. And the headroom is real. Our peak-to-trough utilisation spread is roughly four to one, which means we own capacity sized for a few busy hours a day and let it idle the rest of the time. If we can shift batch workloads into overnight windows, tighten our autoscaling so we're not holding warm capacity against a worst case, and consolidate the small models that currently each claim their own allocation, I believe we can absorb our projected growth for at least two quarters without new silicon. That's two quarters of deferred capital expenditure, which at our scale is not a rounding error.

Latency is the honest counterargument, and I want to take it seriously. Some of our interactive workloads are already brushing against our latency SLOs at peak, and squeezing utilisation typically means higher queueing and more contention. This is the risk I'm least certain about. If a scheduling change pushes p99 latency past what our product teams can tolerate, we'll hear about it quickly and loudly. My proposal is that we treat latency as a hard constraint in the optimisation work: any change that degrades p99 beyond current levels gets rolled back, no exceptions. If we hit that wall — if we genuinely cannot serve interactive demand within SLO on existing hardware — that becomes the clean, evidence-based trigger for a purchase, and we'll make it knowing exactly which workload is driving the need.

Reliability cuts both ways. A larger fleet gives us more redundancy in principle, but our actual failure mode over the past year hasn't been capacity exhaustion; it's been single-node failures that our current orchestration handled poorly. Better bin-packing with tighter affinity rules could actually worsen blast radius if we're careless, so the utilisation work has to include revisiting our placement and failover logic. Done well, a more intelligently scheduled fleet is more resilient than a bigger, dumber one, because we'll finally have theing to drain and rebalance nodes for maintenance instead of running everything on the edge of saturation.

The opportunity cost deserves a sentence of its own. The engineering time this consumes — I'd estimate one engineer for a quarter, plus my own attention — is time not spent on product features. But theing we build (better telemetry, real utilisation dashboards, a scheduler we can actually reason about) pays dividends regardless of what we decide next, and it makes any future purchase smaller and better targeted. Money spent on hardware we don't fully use is gone; time spent understanding our workload is not.

So the recommendation: no new hardware this quarter. Fund a focused utilisation effort with explicit latency guardrails, report back in ninety days with numbers, and let the data make the purchase decision if one is still needed. I'm confident in the direction and genuinely uncertain about the endpoint — which is exactly why we should buy information before we buy iron.

Comments welcome by Friday.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Local AI hardware expansion versus utilisation improvement

**Status and context**

We currently operate a small pool of local accelerators — a handful of high-memory GPUs plus some smaller cards used for experimentation. Over the past quarter, our own telemetry shows the fleet averaging roughly 30–40% utilisation, with sharp peaks around model evaluation runs and long idle stretches overnight and on weekends. At the same time, several teams are queuing for capacity, and the instinct in the room is increasingly "just buy more." This memo argues we should resist that instinct for at least one more quarter, and instead treat utilisation as the primary lever — while being honest about where that argument is weakest.

**The cost picture**

The purchase option is not catastrophic on its face. A single additional high-memory node is a one-time capital expense we could absorb, and prices per unit of compute have been falling. But the sticker price understates the true cost. Power, cooling, rack space, and — most significantly in our environment — the operational burden of managing more hardware fall on a team of four. Every additional device is something we must monitor, patch, and eventually decommission. Meanwhile, the utilisation option costs almost nothing in capital: better scheduling, a shared job queue, and a few weeks of engineering time. If we can lift average utilisation from 35% to 60%, we effectively add half a fleet's worth of capacity for the price of a sprint. That comparison is not exact — peak demand is not average demand, and a busy fleet at 60% may still turn work away at 4pm on a Tuesday — but it establishes the order of magnitude of what's on the table.

**Latency and the shape of our demand**

The strongest argument for buying more hardware is latency: interactive development and fine-tuning experiments feel very different when you wait minutes versus hours. Queuing hurts iteration speed, and iteration speed is where our researchers actually create value. I take this seriously. However, our queue data suggests most delay comes from poor packing and manual reservation habits rather than genuine saturation — jobs are scheduled serially when they could run concurrently, and cards are held by idle notebooks that nobody has released. Fixing the scheduler and introducing automatic preemption of idle sessions attacks exactly the waits people complain about, without new hardware. If, after these changes, the 95th-percentile queue time remains painful, that is a much cleaner signal that demand genuinely exceeds supply, and a purchase at that point would be well-justified rather than premature.

**Reliability and risk**

There is a reliability argument on both sides. More hardware means more redundancy — a failed node is a smaller fraction of total capacity. But a larger fleet also means more failure surface, and our current spare-parts and on-call situation is thin. Improving utilisation on existing hardware, by contrast, forces us to build the scheduling, monitoring, and failover discipline we will need regardless of fleet size. Those are durable assets; an extra GPU is not.

**Opportunity cost and reversibility**

This is where the decision really turns. Capital spent on hardware is largely irreversible — resale value for used accelerators is poor, and the commitment shapes our infrastructure direction for years. Engineering time spent on utilisation is reversible in the best sense: the scheduler, queue, and telemetry we build remain valuable even if we later buy hardware, and they make any future purchase more effective. Buying now forecloses little, but it spends our flexibility. Waiting one quarter costs us some iteration speed in the near term — a real, if modest, opportunity cost — in exchange for a much better-informed decision.

**Recommendation**

Spend the next quarter on utilisation: deploy a proper job queue with preemption, instrument per-team usage, set idle-timeout policies, and publish utilisation dashboards. Set an explicit trigger now — if p95 queue latency for interactive work exceeds an agreed threshold after these changes, we proceed with the purchase without relitigating. This gives the teams waiting on capacity a concrete answer rather than an indefinite "wait and see."

**Uncertainty**

I want to be candid about the limits of this analysis. Our utilisation numbers come from partial instrumentation and may understate real demand; if true utilisation is already near 60%, the case for buying strengthens considerably. We also don't fully know next quarter's demand — a new model line or an urgent evaluation could change the calculus quickly. The trigger mechanism above is designed precisely so that being wrong in either direction is cheap and quickly correctable.

I'd like a decision by end of week so we can start scheduler work immediately.

**— Infrastructure Team**
